title: VLAN
summary: A virtual local area network is a layer two construct that lets one physical switch, or a group of linked switches, carry several logically separate broadcast domains. Each switch port is assigned to a virtual local area network, and frames are tagged between switches using a standard such as the one commonly known as 802.1Q, so devices in different networks cannot reach each other directly even though they share the same hardware. In real environments this separates user, server, voice, management and guest traffic, and it is the practical basis for segmentation and for limiting how far a broadcast storm or an infected host can spread. The mistake people make is assuming the boundary is a security control on its own: traffic between these networks is routed, and if that routing is permissive, or if an attacker can negotiate a trunk port or abuse the untagged native network, the separation provides far less protection than the diagram suggests.

beginner.definition: A VLAN is a way to split one physical network into several separate logical networks. VLAN stands for virtual local area network. Devices in different VLANs behave as if they were plugged into different switches. They need a router to speak to each other.
beginner.whyItMatters: Separating traffic limits the damage when one computer is infected. It also lets you write simple rules, such as allowing guest devices to reach the internet only. A printer or camera on its own network cannot reach your servers. Without this separation, every device shares one crowded and trusting network. The result is that one weak device puts everything else at risk.
howItWorks: The network team decides which groups of devices should stay apart, such as staff and guests.
Each switch port is assigned to one VLAN, and the switch keeps that traffic apart.
When two switches are linked, frames carry a small tag that names their VLAN.
A device in one VLAN can reach another VLAN only through a router or firewall.
That router applies rules that decide which groups may talk and which may not.
Teams review the rules often, because rushed changes can quietly join two groups.
beginner.example: Think of an office with one shared corridor and a single small kitchen. Everyone hears every conversation, and one fire alarm empties the whole floor. Now divide the floor into departments with their own corridors and kitchens, joined by one locked door. Staff still work in the same building, but noise and problems stay inside a department. A VLAN builds those separate corridors inside a network switch.
takeaways: A VLAN separates traffic on shared hardware, but it is not a firewall on its own.
Traffic between VLANs is routed, so the rules on that router are what really protect you.
Review port assignments and trunk links, because a mistake can join two groups silently.

objectives: Explain what a VLAN is and how it differs from a physical network.
Describe how frames are tagged when they travel between switches.
Explain why devices in different VLANs need a router to communicate.
Describe how VLANs support network segmentation and filtering.
Explain why a VLAN alone is not a complete security boundary.
Identify configuration mistakes that weaken the separation.
